knowledge: Evaluate every prospect across five dimensions before making recommendations: (1) What the company does — industry, products/services, whether made/delivered in Canada. This determines which programs are on the table. (2) Revenue — determines eligibility for key programs (CanExport requires $100K+ on last T2/GST return) and which service tier makes sense. (3) Hiring plans — who, when, what type of role, student or full-time, age, field. Opens the entire hiring grant category. (4) Training — are they sending employees to external courses? What kind? Opens training grants. (5) International expansion — selling or planning to sell outside Canada? Which markets? What percentage of revenue? Opens CanExport. Additional factors that significantly affect availability: years in operation (some programs require 1+ year), incorporation status (sole proprietors generally don't qualify), province of registration (affects which provincial programs are accessible), and cash flow capacity (claim-back model requires fronting costs).

Granted focuses on three grant pillars. Pillar 1 — Hiring Grants: Two categories. Student/intern grants cover 50-75% of wages ($2K-$10K per placement), available year-round across semesters, most for post-secondary students in digital/STEM/environmental fields. Canada Summer Jobs works for nearly any position. Graduate/full-time grants cover 50-100% of wages up to $30K, focused on under-30 and digital/tech roles but exceptions exist (WorkBC covers 30+ in BC, newcomer programs cover immigrants regardless of age). Pillar 2 — Training Grants: Reimburse 60-100% of external course costs depending on province and training type. BC offers up to $10K per trainee per year across three streams (foundational up to 100%, technical up to 80%, other up to 60%). Must be third-party training with defined start and end. Pillar 3 — Market Expansion (CanExport): Reimburses approximately 50% of eligible international expansion costs (trade shows, travel, consulting, legal, IP protection, lead generation) up to a maximum of $50K in funding. Requires $100K+ Canadian revenue. Businesses can apply for the US market and reapply for different international markets each year. First-time applicants typically approved for $25-35K in reimbursement.

The most valuable consulting skill is reframing what a prospect THINKS they need into what's actually fundable. Common reframes: 'I need money for equipment/renovations/new location' → Grants don't cover capital expenses. Be empathetic but honest, then pivot: 'What's driving the expansion? Are you hiring to staff the new location? Training people on the new equipment? Expanding into a new market?' Those activities ARE fundable even if the equipment itself isn't. Suggest loan programs (BDC, Black Entrepreneurship Loan) for capital needs. 'I want to expand my business' → Expansion isn't a grant category. Unpack it: the hiring, training, and market entry activities INSIDE the expansion plan are what gets funded. A prospect who says 'I'm expanding' often has 3-4 separate fundable activities they haven't identified. 'I want to hire my contractor full-time' → Potentially fundable, but sequence matters: apply for the grant FIRST, get approved, THEN bring the contractor onto payroll. Cannot apply retroactively. 'My role isn't techy enough' → Many roles that don't sound technical can be reframed. A 'marketing assistant' running digital campaigns and analytics is a digital tech role. A 'bookkeeper' falls under STEM. Focus on the job DESCRIPTION not the title — emphasize the digital and technical components that are genuinely part of the work.

Company size determines the grant strategy. Under $100K revenue, <5 employees: Focus on hiring grants (students/co-ops) and training grants if operating 1+ year. CanExport not available. Recommend GetGranted self-service tier. A small business hiring 2 student interns per year across semesters could access $10-20K in subsidies. $100K-$1M revenue, 5-15 employees: CanExport becomes available. 1-2 student hires per year plus training grants for key upskilling. Pick the top 2-3 programs — bandwidth is limited at this size. $1M-$5M revenue, 15-50 employees: Full range available. Multiple hires, training across teams, CanExport for international growth. Recommend Granted Starter — self-serve platform with 3 grant tokens per year for hiring/training applications. Granted prepares, client submits. This is where strategic planning across all three pillars adds the most value — stacking multiple programs can yield $30-80K+ annually. $5M+ revenue, 50+ employees, 5+ years: Large-scale training budgets, multiple simultaneous hiring grants, complex CanExport projects. Recommend GrantedPro for full-service support. May also qualify for IRAP, SRED, and R&D programs (refer to partners for those). Annual grant potential can exceed $100K with proper planning.

Common scenarios and how to handle them. 'I've never applied before' → Start with the easiest win: a training grant for a course they're already planning, or a hiring grant for a position they're already filling. The process is simpler than they think with guidance. 'I don't think I qualify' → Almost every Canadian business that is hiring, training, or expanding has something available. The issue is usually they don't know what's out there. Ask the five discovery questions — there's almost always at least one grant that fits. 'We have retention problems' → Training grants can help: employees who receive training feel invested in, and team-based training builds cohesion. Grants take the sting off turnover costs. 'I applied before and got rejected' → Large federal grants are extremely competitive (200+ applicants common). Rejection doesn't mean the business is bad. If they received feedback, that's valuable for reapplication. Don't let past rejection discourage them from pursuing other, more accessible grants. 'I'm worried about cash flow' → Take this seriously. Prioritize smaller, faster-reimbursing programs. Some reimburse monthly, others quarterly. If they genuinely cannot front costs, grants may not be the right tool yet — loan programs might be more appropriate first.

When multiple programs apply, prioritize: (1) Time-sensitive programs first — is something about to open or close? Jump on it. (2) Highest dollar value — CanExport at $25-50K typically dwarfs individual hiring grants at $2-10K. (3) Easiest wins — training grants for courses they're already taking are lowest-effort, highest-certainty. Same for hiring grants where the candidate is already identified. (4) Stackable opportunities — can they get both a federal hiring grant AND a provincial one for the same employee? Common stacks: federal SWPP + provincial WorkBC. (5) Pipeline building — even if a program isn't open now, help them prepare so they're ready when it opens. 'CanExport opens in February — let's get your project plan ready now.' The businesses that get the most from grants are the ones who build a year-round strategy layering multiple programs, not the ones who find one program and apply once.

Government funding priorities shift based on federal budget announcements. Current priority areas include: defense and military, tech and AI, infrastructure, green technologies and clean tech, critical minerals, and resources. Programs are increasingly prioritizing applications that align with these areas. For example, CanExport guidelines now explicitly prioritize military and defense-related projects. The strategic insight: if a prospect's business touches any of these priority areas, even tangentially, it strengthens their applications. A construction company using sustainable building methods can be framed as clean tech. A manufacturer whose products could serve defense applications should mention it. The more government priority boxes an application checks (defense + green tech + infrastructure), the stronger the positioning. This doesn't mean fabricating connections — but accurately identifying where a business's activities align with government priorities.

CanExport insider knowledge: Revenue threshold is $100K+ on last CRA T2 and GST return. If a startup is close, a strategic short fiscal year-end can accelerate eligibility. Businesses can apply for the US market and reapply for different international markets each year — there is no limit to how many times you can apply as long as you're targeting different markets. First-time applicants typically get $25-35K, not the full $50K. Critical to understand: CanExport is a 50% cost-share reimbursement model. If a prospect is planning to spend $50K on US expansion (trade shows, travel, market research, consulting), they could receive approximately $25K back in reimbursement, not $25K in free money. Always clarify this when discussing market expansion estimates: 'CanExport would cover roughly half of your expansion costs.' The 'incremental' test is key: activities must be over and above normal operations. Existing contractors on your website/LinkedIn get flagged as operational not incremental. Generic Google/Facebook ads aren't market-specific enough. Content must clearly target the specific market. Longer, more detailed applications with market research perform significantly better. Vague applications ('we know there's a market but don't know our target customer') get rejected immediately. The program is first-come-first-served and highly competitive — start preparing months before the intake opens. There's also a CanExport Innovation stream for R&D with international partners: up to $75K at 75% cost coverage, specifically for developing technology/IP with partners outside Canada.

Critical hiring grant nuances: Most programs require 'net-new' hiring — must hire MORE people than your baseline. Apply BEFORE the employee starts — hiring first then applying = disqualified for most programs. Student grants are structured by semester (May-Aug, Sep-Dec, Jan-Apr); hiring mid-semester means partial funding only. Strategic timing: if hiring in July, consider a 2-month contract first then apply for the September semester for full coverage. It's typically too late to place summer students if it's already May/June — plan for fall. Candidate demographics significantly affect funding: STEM/digital roles get highest availability, followed by green/environmental, youth with barriers (disabilities, mental health), visible minorities/Indigenous/women in underrepresented fields, newcomers/immigrants, then general post-secondary. High school graduates have very limited options (~$2,800 for 3 months). Always verify: Canadian citizen, PR, or protected person — international students do NOT qualify for most programs. Programs from tech bootcamps often have high proportions of international students, so verify every candidate.

Granted doesn't manage R&D grants directly, but the agent should flag opportunities. SRED: federal tax credit reimbursing ~64% of R&D salaries. Critical: founders/developers MUST be on payroll (not sweat equity/contractor) to claim. This is the most common startup mistake — flag it proactively. IRAP: NRC program, practically requires $250K+ revenue and 3-5 FTEs. Each company gets an ITA (Industrial Technology Advisor) — recommend clients email their ITA quarterly with bullet-point updates even when too small to use the program. Out of sight = out of mind. Mitacs: funds research collaborations with universities, good for bringing on research PhDs/master's students. The R&D continuum: (1) Joint IP exploration with collaboration grants like Mitacs (~$75K) — companies must stay at arm's length, don't merge IP prematurely (2) Build phase with IRAP/SRED (3) Market expansion with CanExport. Help clients understand this sequence rather than trying to do everything at once. For R&D specifics, refer to Granted's partner network.
